items.title: Where-used for SAP Build Work Zone content
items.author: WouterLemaire
items.text:
Introduction 
 Do you know in which roles a specific app is used in your SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition site? And which apps are not assigned to any role at all? 
 In the Content Manager you can open a role and see the apps, catalogs, groups and spaces in it. The other direction is a lot harder: starting from an app and finding all the roles, pages, spaces, catalogs and groups that contain it. On a small site you can click through it, on a site with hundreds of apps this is not an option anymore. 
 In this blog post, I'll show you the where-used app I built for this with CAP and Fiori elements, how it works under the hood and how you can run it yourself. 
 Problem 
 The Content Manager is great for building content top down: you create a role, assign apps, add a space with pages. What was missing for me is the view from the bottom up. 
 You need to be able to: 
 Find all roles that give access to an app, directly or through a catalog, group, space or page 
 See the path of that assignment, for example Catalog > Role or Page > Space > Role 
 Find the content that is not in any role, so you can clean it up 
 Jump from one object to the related one without searching over again 
 An app is often assigned in more than one way. It can be in a catalog that is in a role, on a page of a space that is in another role and assigned directly to a third one. That's exactly the information you need before you remove or change something. 
 Solution 
 So I built one: a CAP Node.js service with a Fiori elements List Report and Object Page on top of it, deployed to the HTML5 Application Repository so it can run as a tile in Work Zone itself. 
 My first idea was to read the content live. The Content Manager uses a GraphQL API ( /semantic/graphql ) for this, but that one is internal, not documented and it only answers on the Work Zone admin host. Not something I want to build an app on. So I went for a simpler approach: the app works on an export of the content which you upload in the app. 
 This has a downside, the data is only as fresh as your last import. Nevertheless, it also has an advantage: you can keep an export of each subaccount next to each other as a snapshot and compare dev with production. 
 The best analogy in the SAP world: it's like the where-used list in the ABAP Workbench, but for launchpad content. 
 How it works 
 Before starting on the details, an overview of what happens: 
 You export the content in Work Zone 
 You upload the zip in the app and give it a snapshot name 
 The CAP service reads all content items in the zip and the relations between them 
 It calculates for every item where it is used (directly and indirectly) and stores this in the database 
 The Fiori elements app shows the result 
 The project is small, these are the files that matter: 
 Type File Description 
 Data model db/schema.cds Snapshots, content items and usages 
 Service srv/where-used-service.cds Read-only entities and the import action 
 Handler srv/where-used-service.js Runs the import and replaces an existing snapshot 
 Parser srv/lib/cdm-index.js Reads the export and builds the where-used index 
 UI app/whereused/annotations.cds Fiori elements annotations for the list and the object page 
 UI app/whereused/webapp/ext/ImportAction.js The upload dialog 
 UI app/whereused/webapp/ext/ObjectPageExt.controller.js Navigation from a row to the related object 
 Step 1: Export the content 
 Make an export in the site directory from a specific site to have the full content to look into: 

 This will result in a zip file which contains the content items as JSON documents. 
 Step 2: Import the export 
 In the app, I added a button "Import Export File" on top of the list. This opens a dialog where you select the zip and provide a snapshot name, for example the name of the subaccount: 

 Importing again with the same snapshot name replaces that snapshot, with another name you get a second one next to it. 
 Once imported, the app shows a message with what it found. For the demo content in this blog post it looks like this: 
 24 entities read, 24 items indexed, 29 relations, 66 where-used entries 
 Check this message on your first import, it tells you immediately if the parser understood your file. 
 Step 3: Search 
 The list shows every content item with its type, its ID and the number of roles it ends up in: 

 You can search on title and ID and filter on type, snapshot and number of roles. The red ones are the items that are not in any role. With the filter "Not in any role" you get your cleanup list: 

 In this example the old catalog and the app in it are not used anymore, together with a forgotten PoC app. 
 Step 4: Where is it used? 
 Selecting an item opens the detail page. This one has a table for each type of object the item is used in: roles, pages, spaces, catalogs and groups. 

 The "Customer Overview" app in this example is in two roles, but in three different ways for each of them: through the catalog "Sales Apps" and through two pages in the space "Sales". The column "Path" shows how the app ends up in the role and "Assignment" tells if it is assigned directly or not. 
 Selecting a row brings you to the detail page of that object. So from the app I can open the space, which shows me in the "Contains" table the pages in it: 

 From there you can continue to a page, to a role and so on. The back button brings you back step by step. 
 Under the hood 
 Let's have a look at the three parts that do the real work. 
 The parser 
 The export format is not documented, so I made the parser as generic as possible. It reads every JSON file in the zip (also zips in the zip) and picks up every object that looks like a CDM entity, which means it has an identification with an id and an entityType : 
 const ident = node.identification;
if (ident && typeof ident === 'object' && ident.id && ident.entityType) {
 const key = keyOf(ident.entityType, ident.id);
 const prev = found.get(key);
 // keep the richest version if an entity occurs more than once
 if (!prev || JSON.stringify(node).length > JSON.stringify(prev).length) found.set(key, node);
} 
 The relations between the items come from the relations of each entity. A role has relations to its apps, catalogs, groups and spaces, a space has relations to its pages. The relation of an app to its base app is skipped, that one is not a usage. 
 Pages are a special case. A page doesn't always store its tiles as relations, they are somewhere in the layout of the page. For this, I scan the payload of every page for the IDs of the known apps. Not the most elegant solution, but it works. 
 Once all relations are known, the parser walks from every item upwards to its parents, the parents of the parents and so on. Every object it passes is stored as a usage together with the path to get there. 
 The data model 
 In the data model, every usage is a record "item is used in another item". The trick to get a table for each type on the object page is a set of associations with a filter in the on condition: 
 entity ContentItems : cuid {
 snapshot : Association to Snapshots;
 itemId : String(255);
 itemType : String(30);
 title : String(255);
 description : String(1000);
 providerId : String(255);
 roleCount : Integer default 0;
 isOrphan : Boolean default false;

 usages : Association to many Usages on usages.item = $self;
 roles : Association to many Usages on roles.item = $self and roles.usedInType = 'role';
 catalogs : Association to many Usages on catalogs.item = $self and catalogs.usedInType = 'catalog';
 groups : Association to many Usages on groups.item = $self and groups.usedInType = 'group';
 spaces : Association to many Usages on spaces.item = $self and spaces.usedInType = 'space';
 pages : Association to many Usages on pages.item = $self and (pages.usedInType = 'workpage' or pages.usedInType = 'page');
 contains : Association to many Usages on contains.usedIn = $self and contains.direct = true;
} 
 Each of these associations is a facet on the object page. No custom code required for the tables. Just annotations. 
 The navigation 
 Fiori elements wants to navigate from a table row to a detail page of that row, which would be the usage record. That's not what I want, I want to open the role or the space behind it. This can be done with a controller extension on the object page that overrides onBeforeNavigation : 
 onBeforeNavigation: function (parameters) {
 var context = parameters && parameters.bindingContext;
 var path = context && context.getPath();
 if (!path || !/\/(roles|pages|spaces|catalogs|groups|contains)\(/.test(path)) return false;

 var targetProperty = path.indexOf("/contains(") > -1 ? "item_ID" : "usedIn_ID";
 context.requestProperty(targetProperty).then(function (id) {
 // a plain hash change adds a browser history entry, so Back returns to the item you came from
 if (id) HashChanger.getInstance().setHash("ContentItems(" + id + ")");
 });
 return true; // the default navigation is replaced
} 
 My first version used navigateToRoute of the Fiori elements extension API. The navigation worked, but the back button brought me to the list instead of the previous object. So I changed it to a plain hash change and now the back button behaves as expected 😊 
 Getting It Up and Running 
 Run it locally 
 Clone the repository and install the dependencies: 
 git clone https://github.com/lemaiwo/wz-where-used.git
cd wz-where-used
npm i && (cd app/whereused && npm i) 
 Start the CAP server: 
 cds watch 
 This also serves the UI thanks to the cds-plugin-ui5 , you don't need to start a second server for it. Open http://localhost:4004/be.lemtech.wz.whereused/index.html and log in with the mock user admin / admin (or viewer / viewer for read only). 
 You can validate if everything works by running the unit tests of the parser: 
 npm test 
 Deploy to BTP 
 The project contains an mta.yaml for Cloud Foundry with XSUAA, HANA Cloud (HDI container) and the HTML5 Application Repository: 
 mbt build && cf deploy mta_archives/wz-where-used_1.0.0.mtar 
 Once deployed, your subaccount contains two new role collections: 
 WhereUsedViewer (...) : search and display 
 WhereUsedAdmin (...) : import and delete snapshots as well 
 Next, refresh the HTML5 Apps channel in the Channel Manager of Work Zone and add the app "Work Zone Where-Used" to a role. This makes it available as a tile in your site. 
 Limitations 
 A few things you should know before using it: 
 Snapshot only : the data is as fresh as your last import 
 Page placement is not visibility : a path Page > Space > Role means the tile is on a page of that role. A user only sees the tile if the app is also assigned to the role 
 Role collections are not in the export : Work Zone generates a role collection with the same name as the role, so the role name is your link to the users 
 Titles : in my first real export some apps showed their ID instead of their title, the parser doesn't resolve all title formats yet 
 Undocumented format : the parser is based on what I found in my own exports. If your export looks different, let me know! 
 Conclusion 
 With one upload I now get an answer on "where is this app used?" and "what is not used anymore?" for a complete Work Zone site, without clicking through every role in the Content Manager. CAP and Fiori elements made this a small project: most of the UI is annotations, the only real logic is the parser. 
 Feel free to try it on your own site and let me know what it finds 😉 
 Contributions and feedback are welcome! The full source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/wz-where-used

items.title: Object-Based Authorization (OBA) in SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 – Scheduling & Date Planning adoption
items.author: y4acharya
items.text:
With SAP S/4HANA 2025, SAP introduced Object-Based Authorization (OBA) for Project System, providing a new authorization framework that enables project-level access control beyond traditional role-based security. 
 For a general introduction to Object-Based Authorization, refer to SAP Community's blog on Introducing Object-Based Authorization (OBA) in SA... - SAP Community 
 While SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS00 introduced the OBA framework, SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01 and FPS02 further expands its capabilities: 
 SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01 introduces the Object-Based Authorization (OBA) Deletion Report , (Refer to the SAP Community blog using the link - Introducing Object-Based Authorization (OBA) delet... - SAP Community for more details.) 
 SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 extends OBA support to project scheduling and date planning processes. This enhancement allows organizations to control who can schedule or modify dates for specific project objects , offering a much finer level of authorization than was previously possible. 
 Why is this Enhancement Important? 
 Traditionally, scheduling authorization in SAP Project System was controlled entirely through PFCG role-based authorizations . 
 Although PFCG determines which transactions and actions a user can execute e.g. based on high level organizational assignments, it cannot easily distinguish between individual project objects. 
 For example: 
 A planner may be authorized to execute CJ20N . 
 However, the business may want the planner to schedule Project A but prevent scheduling Project B . 
 Object-Based Authorization addresses this restriction by introducing project object-level authorization . 
 In case OBA is active for a project user must now satisfy both : 
 Standard PFCG authorization 
 Object-Based Authorization (OBA) 
 Only when the right level of privileges is granted to the user scheduling or date-related operations be performed. 

 Project Objects Covered by OBA 
 The scheduling enhancement supports authorization checks across the following Project System objects: 
 Project Definition 
 WBS Elements 
 Networks 
 Activities 
 Activity Elements 
 Subnetworks 
 This ensures authorization is consistently enforced throughout the complete project hierarchy. 
 Prerequisites for Using OBA in Scheduling 
 Before scheduling authorization becomes effective, several configuration steps are required. 
 Step 1 – Activate OBA in the Profile 
 Ensure that Object-Based Authorization is enabled in the appropriate Project Profile or Network Profile before using OBA-enabled scheduling functionality. 
 The activation process is covered in detail in the SAP Community blog " Introducing Object-Based Authorization (OBA) in SA... - SAP Community " and is not repeated here. 
 Step 2 – Configure Message in application area CN 475 in Transaction OBA5 
 Transaction OBA5 determines how the system behaves when a user attempts to schedule an object without sufficient OBA authorization. 
 Message CN 475 controls this behavior. 

 OBA5 Configuration 
 System Behavior 

 Error (E) 
 Scheduling is blocked immediately and message CN475 is issued. 

 Warning (W) 
 Scheduling continues, while message CN475 is logged. 

 Not Configured 
 Defaults to Warning behavior 

 Step 3 – Maintain User Authorizations 
 Assign object-level permissions through the OBA tab. 
 Supported authorization levels include: 
 Read 
 Write 
 Admin 
 No Authorization 
 Permissions can be assigned individually for each project object. 

 Scheduling Scenarios Supporting OBA 
 Project Scheduling 
 Project scheduling performs scheduling across the complete project hierarchy. 
 OBA authorization is validated for: 
 Project Definition 
 WBS Elements 
 Networks 
 Activities 
 Subnetworks 
 WBS Scheduling 
 When scheduling starts from a WBS element, SAP automatically schedules all related child networks and activities. 
 Network Scheduling 
 Object-Based Authorization is also enforced during network scheduling in: 
 CJ20N – Project Builder 
 CN22 – Change Network 
 CN24 – Overall Network Scheduling 
 Authorization checks apply to: 
 Networks 
 Activities 
 Activity Elements 
 Subnetwork 
 Project Planning Board 
 The Project Planning Board (CJ2B) supports several date management functions, including: 
 Reconcile Dates 
 Shift Dates 
 Check Dates 
 Unlike scheduling transactions, these functions primarily synchronize or copy dates rather than execute complete scheduling calculations. 
 Nevertheless, Object-Based Authorization is enforced wherever applicable. 

 Key Points - 
 OBA Complements PFCG 
 Object-Based Authorization does not replace traditional SAP role authorizations. 
 Instead, it introduces an additional layer of security. 
 Users require both: 
 Appropriate PFCG authorizations 
 Required OBA permissions 
 Choosing Between Error and Warning 
 The selection of Error or Warning should align with business requirements. 
 Use Error (E) 
 Recommended when: 
 Strict governance is required. 
 Unauthorized date changes via scheduling must be prevented. 
 Compliance is mandatory. 
 Use Warning (W) 
 Recommended when: 
 Business continuity is more important. 
 Organizations are gradually implementing OBA. 
 Authorization assignments are still being refined. 
 Key Takeaways 
 The adoption of Object-Based Authorization for scheduling in SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 represents a significant enhancement for SAP Project System. 
 Key benefits include: 
 Fine-grained authorization at the project object level 
 Secure scheduling across WBS, networks, activities, and related objects 
 Seamless integration with existing PFCG authorizations 
 Flexible enforcement through configurable OBA5 message handling 
 Improved governance without sacrificing operational flexibility 
 By extending OBA into scheduling and date management, SAP enables organizations to protect critical project planning activities while maintaining the flexibility required for complex project execution.

items.author: Tunir
items.text:
As part of our continued investment in improving the analytics experience for every user, we are excited to share two meaningful improvements to Story Filters in SAP Analytics Cloud: 
 The ability for Story Viewers to Edit Story Filters 
 The first iteration of Add Story Filter support directly within the Lite Viewer 
 Editing Story Filters as a Story Viewer 
 Previously, if a Story Viewer wanted to adjust a Story Filter they had created, the only option was to delete the entire filter and start over. With this release, Story Viewers now see an Edit button directly on their Story Filters, making it quick and easy to modify an existing filter without losing it entirely. 

 We have also extended this capability to Story Filters that were originally created by a Story Designer. If a Story Viewer has the authorization to delete a Story Filter, they can now also edit it. This aligns editing and deletion permissions, keeping the experience predictable and consistent. 
 To make this behaviour transparent to Story Designers, the Input Control Configuration panel now includes a clearly labelled setting: "Allow viewers to edit and delete filter" . This gives designers full visibility and control over what their viewers can do with filters on a given story. 

 Adding and Editing Story Filters in the Lite Viewer 
 For those using the Lite Viewer (for a full introduction to Lite Viewer, see our initial release blog post ), a common friction point has been the need to navigate to the Full Viewer whenever a Story Filter needed to be added. With this release, we are pleased to deliver the first iteration of Story Filter support natively within the Lite Viewer. 
 Story Viewers working within the Lite Viewer can now: 
 Add a Filter by Member directly, without leaving the Lite Viewer 
 Add a Filter by Condition directly, without leaving the Lite Viewer 
 Edit Existing Filters that are based on a Filter by Member or Filter by Condition, without leaving the Lite viewer 

 For Measure and Numeric based Filters and Time Range Filters, the option to redirect to the Full Viewer remains available for now. 

 We are actively working to close these gaps, with Measure and Numeric Filter support planned for the 2027 Q1 QRC. Time Range Filter support will follow in a subsequent release. 

 What's Next 
 These improvements are part of a broader effort to make the Lite Viewer a fully capable analytics experience for Story Viewers, reducing the need to switch between interfaces. We look forward to sharing further updates as we continue to expand Lite Viewer capabilities throughout 2027.

items.title: Thomas Saueressig to Leave SAP Executive Board
items.author: SAP News
items.text:
WALLDORF — SAP SE (NYSE: SAP) today announced that Thomas Saueressig, member of the Executive Board of SAP SE and chief customer officer, has informed the Supervisory Board of his decision to pursue a new opportunity outside the company. 

 All parties agreed that he will remain fully in charge of his current responsibilities until the end of March 2027, ensuring a smooth and seamless transition, with a strong focus on executing the company’s priorities and delivering a successful fourth quarter. 

 Beginning in January, Saueressig will transition his responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, who will assume the role on an interim basis. Raptopoulos, currently global president for EMEA, MEE and APAC and already overseeing key Customer Success organization functions, will ensure continuity across SAP’s customer-facing organizations throughout the transition. The Supervisory Board has initiated the process of determining Saueressig’s succession and will communicate further details in due course. 

 “Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP’s transformation. Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP’s focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future,” said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of SAP SE. 

 “Thomas has played an important role in strengthening how SAP supports customers across their transformation journeys,” said Christian Klein, CEO of SAP SE. “With his deep operational expertise and strong execution mindset, he has helped advance our customer-focused transformation. We thank him for his leadership and his many contributions to SAP.” 

 Saueressig most recently served as chief customer officer, leading SAP’s Customer Value Group, which brings together Sales, Customer Success and Customer Services & Delivery. In this role, he held global responsibility for the entire customer value journey, including cloud operations and infrastructure. Previously, Saueressig oversaw Product & Engineering as a member of SAP’s Executive Board, with global responsibility for all business applications, customer support and cloud operations and infrastructure. 

 Thomas Saueressig joined SAP in 2004 and was appointed to the Executive Board in 2019.

10.summary: Announces that MDK for Windows can call SAP AI Core, with GPT-4o, Gemini and Claude named as example models, so a Windows enterprise app can use these models without custom HTTP code. The post says it covers setup, both native action types, multi-turn chat, tool calling, image generation and safety controls, with code taken from the MDK Demo app. The text provided is only the abstract, so the action type names, configuration steps and code are not visible and cannot be checked here.

The pitch is no custom HTTP code: AI Core is reached through the framework's native actions.
Covered topics: setup, two native action types, multi-turn chat, tool calling, image generation, safety controls.

technical_details: SAP Mobile Development Kit (MDK) for Windows
SAP AI Core as the model access layer
Models named: GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude

10.why_it_matters: For ABAP and mobile developers, this shows AI model calls moving into declarative MDK actions instead of hand-written REST and JSON handling. It also brings model access under AI Core governance, which matters for enterprise rollouts.
10.teaching_angle: Use it to compare a native MDK action with a hand-coded REST call to AI Core: auth, payload shape, error handling, and where safety controls sit. Students can rebuild a single chat turn in the Demo app and then add tool calling.

13.summary: An architecture opinion arguing that moving custom ABAP code to SAP BTP does not by itself give clean core. The author says extensions that still rely on unreleased interfaces, duplicated ERP logic and internal SAP structures just move technical debt to a new location, which the post calls a remote /Z/ namespace. The post promises a better approach, but the text provided does not show what that approach is.
key_points: Relocating custom code to BTP is not the same as achieving clean core.
Dependencies on unreleased interfaces and internal SAP structures keep the debt in place.
Duplicating ERP logic in the extension layer is named as a core anti-pattern.
The post frames the problem as a 'remote /Z/ namespace' and proposes an alternative architecture.
technical_details: Clean core principle in S/4HANA
SAP BTP as side-by-side extension platform
Unreleased vs released interfaces and APIs
Custom namespace /Z/ (and its remote equivalent on BTP)
Internal SAP structures and tables as an anti-pattern
13.why_it_matters: Many teams treat a BTP move as a clean-core fix, and this post pushes back on that. The real test is whether the extension depends only on released contracts and avoids copying ERP logic.
13.teaching_angle: A good discussion piece for interview prep: ask candidates how they would classify an extension that calls an unreleased function module, and what they would replace it with. Pair it with a review of the released API catalogue.

17.summary: Shows that a high cosine similarity score can still return guidance for the wrong SAP edition or release when metadata filters are applied after a global Top-K vector search. The author compares two strategies: filter after global Top-K, and filter first then rank within the eligible set. The post says it uses a reproducible HANA Cloud example and plans a follow-up with a CAP endpoint, stored HANA vectors, applicability mappings and authorization tests.
key_points: Global Top-K followed by a metadata filter can leave no eligible results, or lower-quality ones, even when scores look high.
Filtering first and ranking within the eligible set gives results that fit the user's system.
Applicability mapping (edition/release) and authorization are placed into the CAP search service.
The post is part 1 of a series; the endpoint and request tests are not yet in this text.
technical_details: SAP HANA Cloud vector store and cosine similarity
Top-K vector search
Post-filtering vs pre-filtering on metadata
SAP CAP service for search
Applicability mappings for SAP edition and release
Authorization checks at the service layer
17.why_it_matters: Retrieval for SAP support or migration guidance is wrong if it ranks the wrong release first. This is a common pitfall in RAG on enterprise content, and the fix is a design choice in the query, not a model change.
17.developer_problem: How do I return the closest vector matches only from content that applies to the user's SAP edition and release, without losing relevant results?
17.teaching_angle: A strong exercise for AI-on-SAP courses: write the same query both ways (filter after Top-K, filter before ranking) and show the result sets differ. Discuss why pre-filtering and recall are a trade-off, and where authorization belongs.

26.summary: Explains how an Integration Cell API artifact can identify which external partner is calling when several partners share one URL and each should only see its own data. The author says Basic authentication and default XSUAA tokens do not work for this, because service keys share a client ID and the API artifact replaces the authenticated user with the destination user before custom logic runs. With external OAuth through SAP IAS, the token reaches the artifact unchanged and one claim identifies the partner. The post also covers IAS and API artifact setup and a fallback for partners who cannot use OAuth.
key_points: Basic auth and default XSUAA tokens do not identify the caller: service keys share one client ID.
The API artifact swaps the authenticated user for the destination user before the flow logic runs.
External OAuth via SAP IAS passes the token through unchanged, so the caller can be read from a claim.
The post covers IAS setup, API artifact steps and a fallback for partners who cannot use OAuth.
technical_details: SAP Integration Cell and API artifact
Basic authentication vs OAuth 2.0
SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) as external OAuth provider
XSUAA default tokens and service keys
Destination user mapping in the API artifact
Claim in the IAS token that identifies the partner (claim name not given in the excerpt)
26.why_it_matters: Multi-tenant data separation at the API layer depends on knowing the caller. This post explains why the usual auth options fail for that, which can save a lot of debugging time.
26.developer_problem: How do I find out which external partner is calling a shared Integration Cell API so I can return only that partner's data?
26.teaching_angle: Good case study for integration security: have students trace the request through the API artifact and show where identity is lost. Then ask them to design the IAS token check and a fallback for a partner without OAuth.

86.summary: A blog post by XLC testing SAP Note 3849542, which concerns SAP HANA ALTER TABLE changing stored decimal values. The author reports an ALTER TABLE that succeeds with an unchanged row count while a value changes from 219 to 0.000219. They say they varied precision, scale and compression to find when stored values changed. The lead promises the workaround cost in a 100-million-row test and evidence for judging whether data was affected. Only the introduction is included here, so the actual test matrix, results and workaround figures are not visible.
key_points: Symptom: an ALTER TABLE on a decimal column succeeds, the row count is unchanged, and stored values are altered (219 becomes 0.000219).

digest.headline: A thin day for core ABAP: clean-core and released-API questions, a HANA ALTER TABLE decimal risk, and RAG pre-filtering lead the material.
digest.overview:
Most of today's material is community Q&A and blog introductions with little code. The strongest items are a XLC investigation of SAP Note 3849542, where a HANA ALTER TABLE on a decimal column succeeds with an unchanged row count but changes stored values (219 to 0.000219) [86]. Also strong are an opinion post arguing that BTP is not a clean-core fix in itself [13], and a forum question about replacing the unreleased FM CK_F_CSTG_STRUCTURE_EXPLOSION [44]. Several posts give only abstracts, so their technical content cannot be checked.

For ABAP trainers, the recurring problems are released-API discipline, reading generic gateway errors (the purchase contract item POST [97]), BAdI-driven UI extension that does not show up [106], and sy-subrc semantics after method calls [53]. A vector-search post shows that filter-then-rank differs from rank-then-filter [17]. That is a query design point you can teach without any model knowledge.

top_stories.title: HANA ALTER TABLE may change decimal values silently (SAP Note 3849542)
top_stories.summary: XLC reports an ALTER TABLE on a DECIMAL column that succeeds with the row count unchanged, while a stored value changes from 219 to 0.000219. The author varied precision, scale and compression and costed a workaround on 100 million rows. Only the introduction is available, so the results are not visible.
top_stories.why_it_matters: A DDL that reports success can still alter data. Verify values (aggregates or checksums) before and after decimal changes, and read the SAP Note itself.

top_stories.title: BTP is not automatically clean core
top_stories.summary: The post argues that moving custom code to BTP only relocates technical debt if it still uses unreleased interfaces, duplicates ERP logic or depends on internal SAP structures. It calls this a 'remote /Z/ namespace'. The alternative it proposes is not visible in the excerpt.
top_stories.why_it_matters: The test for clean core is dependence on released contracts, not where the code runs.

top_stories.title: Replacement for unreleased FM CK_F_CSTG_STRUCTURE_EXPLOSION
top_stories.summary: A team building a Fiori/RAP cost estimate item report needs a full standard cost estimate breakdown (structure, activities, work centres, cost centres, prices). The FM they use is not released. The post has no answer yet.
top_stories.why_it_matters: It is a typical clean-core case: no obvious released object covers the need, so you must check release state and decide what to do next.

top_stories.title: Vector search: filter before ranking, not after
top_stories.summary: On HANA Cloud, a global Top-K followed by a metadata filter can return nothing eligible, or poorer results, even with high cosine scores. Filtering by edition and release first, then ranking, fits the user's system. Authorization and applicability mapping sit in the CAP service.
top_stories.why_it_matters: It is a query design fix, not a model change, and it applies to any retrieval over release-specific SAP content.

top_stories.why_it_matters: It explains why common auth options fail for per-partner data separation.

deep_dives.title: Validating DDL on HANA decimal columns
deep_dives.explanation:
The XLC post describes an ALTER TABLE on a DECIMAL column that completes with no error and an unchanged row count, yet a stored value changes from 219 to 0.000219 [86]. The author varied precision, scale and compression to find when values change. Only the introduction is available, so the conditions are not confirmed here. Read SAP Note 3849542 for the affected releases and the fix.

The practical lesson is about what counts as proof. A row count only shows that rows survived. For numeric columns, take an aggregate snapshot before the change, such as `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(col)`, `MIN(col)` and `MAX(col)`, and compare it afterwards. For critical tables, a checksum over the key and the value columns is stronger.

For ABAP teams the exposure is in table changes made through DDIC activation and conversions, and in direct DDL on custom tables. Test a copy of the table first. The post also costs a workaround on 100 million rows, so plan the downtime and the verification time together.

deep_dives.title: Debugging a generic OData gateway error on the purchase contract API
deep_dives.explanation:
The post shows a deep insert into `A_PurchaseContract` (API_PURCHASECONTRACT_PROCESS_SRV v0002) that works, including nested `to_PurContrItemCndnValdty` and `to_PurContrItmCndnAmount`. A later POST to `A_PurchaseContract('4600000066')/to_PurchaseContractItem` for item 20 fails with `/IWBEP/CM_MGW_RT/188` 'Service provider did not return any business data' [97].

That message is generic. Take the transaction ID and timestamp from the response and look in `/IWFND/ERROR_LOG` on the hub, then the backend error log, for the real business message. The post cuts off before this.

Three things in the post are worth checking. First, item 20 was already in the creation payload, so confirm whether it exists on the contract, because a duplicate item number is a plausible cause. Second, the failing payload has FRA1 and RA00 but no PB00, which the working one included. Third, RA00 has ConditionCurrency '%', which should be compared to the condition type configuration. None of these is confirmed in the post.

The general method is to compare the working and failing requests field by field, check `$metadata` for what the navigation supports, and retest with the smallest payload.

deep_dives.title: Filter-first vs filter-after in HANA vector search
deep_dives.explanation:
The post compares two query shapes for a vector search over SAP guidance content. In the first, a global Top-K is taken by cosine similarity and metadata filters (edition, release) are applied afterwards. In the second, the filter is applied first and ranking happens within the eligible set [17].

The first shape can return fewer results than K, or none, because the best global matches belong to other releases. High scores do not mean the match applies to the user's system. The second shape returns the best matches among applicable content.

The author places applicability mapping and authorization in the CAP search service, so access control is part of the query and not an afterthought. A follow-up with the endpoint and tests is announced. The exact SQL is not in the excerpt, so reproduce it yourself on a HANA Cloud trial.

The ABAP parallel is a familiar one: a WHERE clause that restricts the data before a ranking or `UP TO n ROWS` is not the same as limiting after the fact.

interview_questions.question: An ALTER TABLE on a HANA decimal column succeeds and the row count is the same. How do you confirm that no data was altered?
interview_questions.answer: A row count only shows that rows exist, not that values are intact. A recent XLC investigation of SAP Note 3849542 reports a value changing from 219 to 0.000219 with no error. I would take a snapshot before the change: COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX on the numeric columns, grouped by a sensible key. For critical tables I would add a checksum over key and value columns. After the change I compare the same figures and sample rows. I would run this on a copy first, check the SAP Note for affected releases, and plan time for a workaround on large tables.

interview_questions.question: A deep insert into an OData V2 API works, but a later POST to a child navigation fails with /IWBEP/CM_MGW_RT/188. How do you analyse it?
interview_questions.answer: The message is generic and does not carry the business reason. I take the transaction ID and timestamp from the response and look in /IWFND/ERROR_LOG on the hub, then the backend log, for the real message. Then I compare the working and failing payloads field by field. In the purchase contract case, item 20 may already exist from the deep insert, and the failing payload has no PB00 condition. I would also check $metadata for what the navigation supports, and retry with the smallest valid payload. The create path and the add-item path should be tested separately.

interview_questions.question: A team wants to replace an unreleased function module in a custom Fiori/RAP report. How do you approach it under clean core?
interview_questions.answer: First I confirm the release state of the object in ADT, through its API state. Then I look for a released CDS view or released API that covers the data, using the released object catalogue. If none exists, I consider a custom CDS view on released sources, or document a justified exception with a fallback and an owner. I avoid moving the call to BTP and treating that as a fix, because it carries the same unreleased dependency. The decision and its reasoning should be recorded so that upgrades can be checked against it.
